before: ABSTRACT: Large-language-model agents need an execution environment that manages conversations, invokes tools, coordinates work, and preserves application state. This report presents the design and evaluation of a multi-tenant agent runtime with financial research applications. The runtime supports staged single-agent execution and optional coordinator–specialist collaboration through a common set of session, scheduling, tool, and persistence mechanisms. Authenticated access, bounded execution, cancellation, and execution traces provide control over the model–tool interaction cycle. Financial applications combine deterministic data processing with model interpretation in four workflows: earnings-event review, candidate screening, portfolio risk diagnosis, and the handling of conflicting or incomplete evidence. These workflows connect source material and analytical conclusions to persistent research records or diagnostic outputs. Evaluation combines executable mechanism tests, repeated comparisons of execution modes, and end-to-end application studies. The results identify trade-offs in completion, latency, evidence retention, and resource use, while selected analyses of public disclosures illustrate useful financial interpretation. The project demonstrates how a reusable runtime can support inspectable financial research workflows, with analytical quality remaining dependent on the model, available evidence, and task design.
after: Abstract—Large language model agents need a runtime to manage conversations, execute tools, coordinate tasks, and save application state. This report presents the design and evaluation of a multi-tenant agent runtime with financial research applications. The runtime supports staged single-agent execution and optional collaboration between a coordinator and specialists. Both modes use the same session, scheduling, tool, and storage mechanisms. Authentication, execution limits, cancellation, and traces help control and inspect each task. Four financial workflows use these mechanisms: earnings-event review, candidate screening, portfolio risk diagnosis, and review of conflicting or incomplete evidence. Deterministic tools process data and calculations, while the model interprets the evidence and proposes research decisions. Evaluation covers runtime tests, repeated Solo and Team comparisons, and end-to-end application cases. The results show trade-offs in completion, latency, evidence retention, and resource use. Selected analyses of public disclosures also show how the system can produce useful research outputs. Their quality still depends on the model, available evidence, and task design.

before: Large language models (LLMs) can answer questions, generate code, and invoke external tools, but model capability alone does not produce a dependable software system. A practical agent must receive requests from multiple interfaces, preserve conversation state, decide which capabilities are available, execute tools under policy, recover from partial failure, stream progress to users, and leave an auditable record. In a multi-user deployment, these concerns expand to authentication, per-tenant data isolation, cancellation, concurrency control, and protection against cross-agent cycles or runaway delegation.
after: Large language models (LLMs) can answer questions, generate code, and invoke tools. A dependable agent also needs software to manage the work around those calls. It must receive requests, preserve conversation history, enforce tool permissions, handle failures, and stream progress to users. A multi-user service must also authenticate callers, isolate their data, control concurrency, and cancel work when requested. Delegation adds another concern: agents must not create circular waits or repeat tasks without limit.

before: The reasoning–action–observation pattern introduced by ReAct [1] provides a useful conceptual basis: the model alternates between reasoning, external action, and observation until it can produce a final answer. However, ReAct describes an interaction pattern rather than a production runtime. The engineering challenge is to turn that pattern into a controlled state machine whose transitions are observable and testable. A model request can fail, a tool can time out, the client can disconnect, a session can contain an unmatched tool result, or a coordinator can repeatedly call the same specialist. Without runtime-level rules, these failures are easily mistaken for “model intelligence” problems.
after: ReAct [1] describes a cycle in which a model reasons, takes an external action, and uses the resulting observation to decide what to do next. A runtime turns this interaction pattern into an execution process that can be controlled and tested. It must handle failed model requests, tool timeouts, client disconnections, and incomplete conversation histories. It must also manage repeated specialist calls. These are execution problems that cannot be assessed from the final answer alone.

This project therefore uses BFCL-style cases as protocol checks rather than reporting an official BFCL score.

before: The design follows fail-safe defaults, complete mediation, and least privilege as classical protection principles [12]. Every protected ingress must resolve an identity; agent selection is checked after default resolution; policy removes denied tools before the model sees them; trusted user scope is carried outside model-controlled arguments; and sandbox startup failure does not silently enable host execution. before: Internal sub-agent work inherits the root execution identifier. It does not acquire a second global semaphore slot, which prevents a coordinator from deadlocking when the configured maximum concurrency is one. Two independent bounds apply: the TaskQueue owns a 256-slot internal admission channel, and the MessageBus owns a separate 256 pending-correlation cap. They protect different resources and must be tuned together. The local completion callback is published at most once, but model calls, external side effects, and network delivery are not guaranteed to occur exactly once. Internal tasks retain request metadata while rebuilding cancellation links to both the request and queue shutdown. Retaining only the original cancellation chain could end nested telemetry too early; detaching it without new links would leave internal work running after its parent stops.

before: The database is mandatory. SQLite with write-ahead logging is the zero-configuration default. before: Session-history compaction is a bounded-context safeguard, not a replacement for durable conversation storage. The current Go implementation estimates tokens from message text and tool-call arguments and checks an 80,000-token threshold at turn entry. When the estimate crosses that threshold, it first logs the full history and replaces long tool results older than the most recent 20 messages with a short marker. If pruning is insufficient, it asks the configured model to summarize the older messages while retaining those recent messages. A summarization failure falls back to the pruned history. This two-stage policy reduces repeated tool-output payloads before it abstracts conversational decisions, but its approximate token estimate and model-generated summary do not guarantee preservation of every earlier fact. It is distinct from the SEC experiment's retrieval stage, which selects source records into an Evidence Bundle; the experiment uses isolated sessions and does not evaluate session-history compaction as a treatment.
